blocks.text: The Fundamentals module introduced tools briefly as one of the three things a server can expose, alongside resources and prompts. This lesson goes deep on that one concept specifically, since tools are usually the single most important part of any MCP server, they are what actually let a model take action in the world, rather than just talk about it.
1. A Tool Is an Action, Not Just Data

blocks.alt: A tool is compared against a resource, which is data

blocks.text: The single most important thing to understand about a tool is that calling it is expected to do something, send an email, create a record, run a calculation, possibly changing state somewhere in the world. This is the core distinction from a resource, which is meant to be read, not acted upon, keeping this "do versus read" line clear is the fastest way to decide whether a piece of functionality belongs in the tools bucket or the resources bucket.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: Ask yourself, does calling this change something in the world, or does it just show me something that already exists, the former is a tool, the latter is a resource.

blocks.text: This distinction is not just academic, it directly affects how carefully a server author needs to think about permissions, retries, and side effects, none of which matter nearly as much for something that only ever reads.
2. The Four Parts of Every Tool

blocks.alt: A name, description, input schema, and handler make up a tool

blocks.text: Every tool has the same four parts, a name that identifies it uniquely on that server, a description written in plain language explaining what it does and when to use it, an inputSchema describing exactly what arguments it accepts, and a handler, the actual code that runs when the tool is called and produces a result.
Most MCP SDKs let a developer define all four parts together in one place, often using a decorator or registration function, rather than assembling this JSON structure by hand.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Part","Purpose"],"rows":[["name","Unique identifier"],["description","Tells the model when and why to use it"],["inputSchema","Defines valid arguments"],["handler","Executes the actual logic"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why the Description Matters More Than You Would Think

A model decides whether and when to call a tool almost entirely based on its name and description, a vague description like "handles emails" gives the model far less to work with than a specific one like "send an email to a specified recipient with a subject and body," clear, specific descriptions measurably improve how reliably a model picks the right tool at the right moment.

code.content:
# vague vs specific descriptions, same tool
# vague: "Handles emails"
# specific: "Sends an email to a given recipient with a subject and body, use this when the user explicitly asks to send or notify someone by email"

blocks.text: A specific description also helps a human developer debugging the system later, quickly understanding what a tool is for without needing to read its implementation code.
4. Tools Are Discovered, Not Assumed

A client never hardcodes which tools a server has, it always asks first, using the tools/list method, this is what allows a server to add, remove, or change tools over time without every connected client needing advance notice or a code change.
This same discovery call typically happens once at the start of a session, though a well-behaved client can call it again if the server sends a notification indicating its tool list has changed.
This same pattern extends naturally, a server can be upgraded with an entirely new tool overnight, and every client already connected will simply see it appear the next time it lists tools.
5. Calling a Tool: tools/call

blocks.alt: A client sends tools/call to the server

blocks.text: Once a model, through the host, decides to use a specific tool, the client sends a tools/call request naming that tool and supplying arguments matching its inputSchema, the server runs its handler and sends back a result.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["name","Which tool to call"],["arguments","The input values matching that tool's inputSchema"]]}

blocks.title: Where the result goes
blocks.content: The tool result is handed back to the model as fresh context, letting it continue reasoning with real, current information rather than relying only on what it already knew.

blocks.text: 6. Side Effects Are the Point, and the Risk

blocks.alt: A tool call produces a real side effect

blocks.text: Because tools genuinely change things, sending a real email, charging a real payment, deleting a real file, they carry real risk if called incorrectly or unexpectedly. This is exactly why permission scoping, covered in the Tool Permissions lesson later in this module, matters so much more for tools than it typically does for read-only resources.

This is also why a server author should think carefully about what happens if a tool is called with unexpected, though technically schema-valid, arguments, like an empty string where a real value was expected.

blocks.title: A guiding question
blocks.content: Before calling a real, side-effecting tool, it is worth asking, what is the blast radius if this call happens by mistake, a small blast radius needs less caution than a large one.

blocks.text: Some teams keep a simple internal list distinguishing read-only tools from side-effecting ones, making it easy to apply stricter review or extra confirmation only where it is actually needed.
7. Idempotent vs Non-Idempotent Tools

blocks.alt: An idempotent tool is safe to repeat while a non-idempotent tool changes each time

blocks.text: An idempotent tool produces the same effect no matter how many times it is called with the same arguments, checking a weather forecast twice does not double the weather, a non-idempotent tool does not have this property, sending the same email twice sends two emails. Knowing which category a tool falls into matters enormously when deciding whether it is safe to automatically retry a failed call.
Many APIs support an idempotency key specifically to make an otherwise non-idempotent action safely retryable, a well-designed tool wrapping such an API should pass that key through consistently.
Marking a tool clearly as one or the other, even just in its description, helps both human reviewers and any automated retry logic make the right call about when a retry is safe.

code.content:
# a supporting idempotency key pattern
result = client.call_tool("charge_payment", {"amount": 500, "idempotency_key": "order-8213"})
# a retry with the same key is safely recognized as the same original request

blocks.text: 8. Naming Tools Clearly and Consistently

A good tool name is a short, specific verb phrase, send_email, create_ticket, search_documents, rather than a vague noun like email or ticket, a clear, action-oriented name reinforces to the model, and to any human reading the tool list, exactly what calling it will cause to happen.
Consistency across a whole server matters too, if one tool is named create_ticket, a related tool should probably be close_ticket, not something inconsistent like ticket_shutdown.

A short prefix convention, like calendar_create_event versus email_send, can also help a model, and a human, quickly tell which underlying system a tool belongs to when a server exposes many tools at once.
9. One Tool, One Job

blocks.alt: A narrow, focused tool is compared against a broad, overloaded tool

blocks.text: A well-designed tool typically does one clear thing, rather than one giant tool with a mode parameter that switches between many unrelated behaviors, several small, focused tools are usually easier for a model to reason about correctly, and easier for a server author to test and secure independently.

blocks.title: A useful design test
blocks.content: If describing a tool naturally requires the word "or" more than once, it is often a sign the tool should be split into two or more focused tools instead.

code.content:
# harder to reason about
{"name": "manage_ticket", "inputSchema": {"properties": {"action": {"enum": ["create", "close", "delete"]}}}}
# easier to reason about
# separate tools: create_ticket, close_ticket, delete_ticket

blocks.text: This principle mirrors good function design in ordinary software engineering, a function that does one clear thing is easier to test, reuse, and reason about than one that branches into several unrelated behaviors.
10. Tools That Wrap an Existing System

Most real tools are thin wrappers around something that already exists, a database query, a third-party API call, a local file operation, the tool’s job is simply to expose that existing capability through the standard MCP shape, not to reimplement the underlying functionality from scratch.

code.content:
def send_email_handler(to, subject, body):
    return smtp_client.send(to=to, subject=subject, body=body)   # wraps existing email infrastructure

blocks.text: This wrapping relationship is exactly why building a new MCP server is often much faster than it sounds, most of the actual logic already exists, the work is mainly in describing it well and exposing it through the standard shape.
11. Tools and the Model's Reasoning Loop

In an agentic workflow, a model often calls a tool, examines the result, and decides what to do next, possibly calling another tool, this loop, think, act, observe, repeat, is the foundation of how AI agents accomplish multi-step tasks, and every step of "act" in that loop is, in an MCP-based system, a tool call.
This loop is precisely why tool result quality matters so much, a vague or incomplete result forces the model to guess at what to do next, while a clear one lets it proceed confidently.
12. Returning Rich Results, Not Just Success or Failure

blocks.alt: A tool result carries rich, structured data

blocks.text: A tool result is most useful to a model when it returns real, specific information, not just a bare success flag, a create_ticket tool that returns the new ticket ID and a link is far more useful to a model continuing a multi-step task than one that simply returns true.

code.content:
# a rich result the model can actually use in its next step
{"ticket_id": "T-4821", "url": "https://tickets.example.com/T-4821", "status": "open"}

blocks.text: A rich result also makes debugging far easier, a log line showing the exact ticket ID and URL returned is much more useful after the fact than one that only says the call succeeded.
This principle scales down too, even a simple confirmation tool benefits from returning a small amount of specific detail, a timestamp, an ID, rather than a bare true.
13. Timeouts and Long-Running Tools

A tool that takes a long time to complete, generating a report, processing a large file, needs special handling so it does not block the whole session, this is covered in full in the Async Tools lesson later in this module, for now it is enough to know that a tool author should think about how long a call realistically takes before assuming a simple, synchronous request-response shape is sufficient.
A client that never accounts for a possible timeout risks leaving a user, or a model, waiting indefinitely on a call that will never return in a reasonable amount of time.

A reasonable default is to set a generous but finite timeout, and to design genuinely slow operations, like generating a large report, as asynchronous from the start rather than forcing them into a synchronous shape.

Communicating an estimated duration in the tool description itself, such as noting a report generation tool may take several minutes, also helps a host application set sensible expectations before the call even starts.
14. A Worked Example
Trace a two-tool sequence, searching for a document and then summarizing it, showing how the result of the first call becomes an input to reasoning about the second.

code.content:
results = client.call_tool("search_documents", {"query": "quarterly report"})
top_doc_id = results["documents"][0]["id"]
content = client.call_tool("get_document", {"id": top_doc_id})
print(content["text"][:200])

blocks.text: Notice that the model never needed to know how search_documents or get_document were implemented internally, it only needed their names, descriptions, and the shape of their results to chain them together correctly.

blocks.title: Trace it yourself
blocks.content: Try rewriting this example with a third tool call, sending the summary somewhere, and notice how naturally it extends the same discover-call-observe pattern.

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes When Designing Tools

items: Writing a vague tool description that leaves a model guessing at when the tool is appropriate to use.
Bundling too many unrelated behaviors into a single tool controlled by a mode or type parameter, instead of separate, focused tools.
Forgetting whether a tool is idempotent, and retrying a non-idempotent one automatically after a timeout, potentially causing a duplicate real-world effect.
Exposing a dangerously broad tool, like one that can delete arbitrary records, without any additional permission gate in front of it.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is returning a bare success or failure boolean from a tool when returning specific, structured details would let the model make much better decisions about what to do next.

A sixth common mistake is naming two different tools almost identically, like update_ticket and modify_ticket, when only one should exist, this kind of near-duplicate naming confuses a model choosing between them.
A seventh common mistake is skipping the description entirely and relying only on the tool name, even a short, well-chosen name rarely conveys as much useful context as one good sentence can.
16. Practice: Design Three Tools for a Task Manager

Sketch tool descriptions and inputSchemas for three tools a simple task-management MCP server might expose, creating a task, marking a task complete, and listing open tasks, paying attention to clear naming and focused, single-purpose scope for each one.
Once you have sketched these three, consider whether any of them are non-idempotent, and if so, what would happen if the same call were accidentally sent twice.
As a final step, write a one sentence description for each of your three tools, specific enough that a model unfamiliar with your task manager would still know exactly when to reach for each one.
Key Takeaway

A tool is an action a model can invoke, defined by a name, a description, an inputSchema, and a handler, discovered dynamically rather than hardcoded, and called through the standard tools/call request, since tools have real side effects, clear naming, focused scope, and careful permission handling matter more here than almost anywhere else in an MCP system.

This lesson builds on the brief introduction to tools from earlier in this module, and connects forward to the Resources lesson next, which covers the read-only counterpart to everything just discussed here.

The rich-results principle from the newly added section is one of the most impactful, easy-to-apply improvements a tool author can make, a small amount of extra detail in a result often saves the model an entire additional round trip.
